[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021029] Published Thu May 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates gate-tunable ballistic spin transport in graphene using transverse magnetic focusing, enabling coherent spin control via electron optics.
motivation: To achieve coherent spin control in graphene for spintronic applications, leveraging ballistic transport and electron optics.
method: Transverse magnetic focusing in encapsulated graphene devices, with gate-tunable control of spin transport.
result: Observation of ballistic spin transport and coherent spin control through spin-dependent electron optics.
conclusion: Provides a mechanism for spin-based devices in graphene, with potential for future spintronic circuits.

title: Breakdown Of The Thermodynamic Limit In Quantum Spin And Dimer Models
authors: Jeet Shah, Laura Shou, Jeremy Shuler, And Victor Galitski
abstract:
Author(s): Jeet Shah, Laura Shou, Jeremy Shuler, and Victor Galitski

Geometry-induced quantum phase separation in quantum dimer models demonstrates that domain shape can fundamentally alter macroscopic ground states, challenging traditional assumptions about the thermodynamic limit.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021020] Published Mon Apr 27, 2026.
tldr: This paper shows that geometry-induced quantum phase separation in quantum dimer models can break the thermodynamic limit, meaning macroscopic ground states depend on domain shape.
motivation: To challenge the traditional assumption that macroscopic properties are independent of system shape in the thermodynamic limit, by studying quantum dimer models.
method: Analytical and numerical analysis of quantum dimer models on lattices with different domain shapes, examining ground state properties and phase separation.
result: Domain shape can fundamentally alter macroscopic ground states, leading to quantum phase separation that violates the thermodynamic limit.
conclusion: The findings suggest that in certain quantum spin and dimer models, the thermodynamic limit may not hold, with implications for understanding quantum phases and phase transitions.

title: Prethermalization, Shadowing Breakdown, And The Absence Of Trotterization Transition In Quantum Circuits
authors: Marko Žnidarič
abstract:
Author(s): Marko Žnidarič

New research uses truncated propagators to show that shadowing time in many-body chaotic systems is finite. It also offers a method to calculate thermalization time, finding that the “Trotterization transition” is generically a finite-size effect.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021017] Published Wed Apr 22, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies prethermalization and shadowing breakdown in quantum circuits, showing that the Trotterization transition is a finite-size effect.
motivation: To understand the dynamics of many-body chaotic systems under Trotterized evolution and to clarify whether a Trotterization transition exists in the thermodynamic limit.
method: The author uses truncated propagators to analyze shadowing time and thermalization time in quantum circuits.
result: Shadowing time is finite in many-body chaotic systems, and the Trotterization transition is generically a finite-size effect, not a true phase transition.
conclusion: The findings imply that Trotter error does not lead to a sharp transition in the thermodynamic limit, which has implications for quantum simulation and digital quantum computing.

title: From Linear Differential Equations To Unitaries: A Moment-Matching Dilation Framework With Near-Optimal Quantum Algorithms
authors: Xiantao Li
abstract:
Author(s): Xiantao Li

Mapping ancillary degrees of freedom to a one-dimensional tight-binding lattice overcomes traditional connectivity bottlenecks, enabling the near optimal quantum simulation of nonunitary dynamics.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020350] Published Thu Jun 04, 2026.
tldr: A framework using a tight-binding lattice to map ancillary degrees of freedom enables near-optimal quantum simulation of nonunitary dynamics.
motivation: To overcome connectivity bottlenecks in quantum simulation of nonunitary dynamics, which are important for open quantum systems and linear differential equations.
method: The paper introduces a moment-matching dilation framework that maps ancillary degrees of freedom to a one-dimensional tight-binding lattice, enabling efficient simulation.
result: The framework achieves near-optimal quantum algorithms for simulating nonunitary dynamics, improving over previous methods.
conclusion: The work provides a practical approach to simulate nonunitary processes on quantum computers, with potential applications in quantum chemistry and physics.

title: Nontrivial Multiproduct Commutation Relation Toward Reducing $T$-Count In Sequential Pauli-Based Computation
authors: Yusei Mori, Hideaki Hakoshima, And Keisuke Fujii
abstract:

By harnessing nontrivial commuting structures in quantum circuits, a novel multiproduct commutation relation significantly reduces the costly
[PRX Quantum 7, 020345] Published Mon Jun 01, 2026.
tldr: The paper introduces a multiproduct commutation relation to reduce T-count in sequential Pauli-based computation, a fault-tolerant quantum computing technique.
motivation: T-gates are costly in fault-tolerant quantum computation, and reducing T-count is crucial for practical quantum advantage.
method: The authors derive a nontrivial multiproduct commutation relation that allows more efficient compilation of quantum circuits by exploiting commuting structures.
result: The proposed relation significantly reduces the number of T-gates required in sequential Pauli-based computation.
conclusion: This work provides a new tool for quantum circuit optimization, potentially improving the feasibility of fault-tolerant quantum algorithms.

title: Transversal Architecture For Megaquop-Scale Quantum Simulation With Neutral Atoms

motivation: To enable large-scale quantum simulation with error correction, addressing overhead challenges in logical layout, space, and time.
method: Integration of a space-time efficient small-angle rotation error correction architecture with neutral-atom hardware, extended to high-rate codes.
result: Significant savings in logical layout, space, and time overhead for quantum simulation.
conclusion: The architecture paves the way for practical megaquop-scale quantum simulation with neutral atoms.

abstract:

[PRX Quantum 7, 020341] Published Thu May 28, 2026.
tldr: This paper defines and quantifies Majorana bound states in interacting systems, focusing on their robustness and locality for non-Abelian braiding.
motivation: Recent quantum-dot experiments motivate a rigorous definition of Majorana bound states in interacting systems to assess their protection and feasibility for topological quantum computing.
method: The authors develop theoretical criteria to quantify robustness and locality of Majorana bound states in the presence of interactions, likely using numerical simulations or analytical models.
result: The paper provides a framework to evaluate how interactions affect the protection and non-Abelian properties of Majorana bound states.
conclusion: The work offers tools to guide experiments on Majorana-based qubits, but its direct relevance to the user's interests in information thermodynamics, quantum foundations, communication, or hybrid systems is limited.

result: An efficient quantum algorithm is provided that generalizes previous hidden subgroup algorithms to the state setting, with applications to learning stabilizer groups.

[PRX Quantum 7, 020331] Published Mon May 18, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies string-breaking dynamics in quantum adiabatic and diabatic processes, focusing on confinement in lattice gauge theories.
motivation: To understand the real-time dynamics of string breaking in confining gauge theories, which is relevant for quantum simulation of high-energy physics.
method: The authors use a trapped-ion quantum simulator to emulate a spin chain with long-range interactions that map to a lattice gauge theory, and they probe string-breaking dynamics via adiabatic and diabatic protocols.
result: They observe regimes where strings do not simply break but exhibit complex quantum dynamics, including multi-string states and non-equilibrium effects.
conclusion: The work provides new insights into confinement dynamics and demonstrates the capability of quantum simulators to explore non-perturbative phenomena in gauge theories.

title: Efficient Simulation Of Logical Magic State Preparation Protocols
authors: Samyak Surti, Lucas Daguerre, And Isaac H. Kim
abstract:

tldr: The paper presents an efficient classical simulation method for logical magic state preparation protocols by propagating errors to the end of the circuit.
motivation: To enable scalable classical simulation of logical magic state preparation, which is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computing but typically computationally expensive.
method: The authors develop a technique that propagates errors through the circuit to the final measurement, reducing the simulation complexity for a large class of protocols.
result: The method makes classical simulation of logical magic state preparation scalable and efficient, allowing verification of protocols that were previously intractable.
conclusion: This work provides a practical tool for designing and verifying magic state preparation protocols, advancing fault-tolerant quantum computing.

authors: Hsiang-Ku Lin, Pak Kau Lim, Alexey A. Kovalev, And Leonid P. Pryadko

conclusion: These codes offer a practical advantage for fault-tolerant quantum computing, though further study is needed for implementation.

motivation: To develop a general and efficient protocol for preparing multimode multi-photon quantum states, which are important for quantum information processing.

title: Quantum Error-Corrected Computation Of Molecular Energies

method: The authors use noise-aware calibration, logical rotation gates, and quantum error-correction gadgets to implement a partially fault-tolerant algorithm for computing molecular energies on a trapped-ion quantum processor.
result: They successfully compute molecular energies with improved accuracy compared to non-error-corrected approaches, demonstrating the feasibility of error-corrected quantum chemistry.

By generalizing from qubit error correction, fault-tolerant protocols tailored to fermionic processes are created, which enable gates, measurements, and codes.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020315] Published Fri Apr 24, 2026.
tldr: This paper develops fault-tolerant protocols for Majorana-based quantum codes, focusing on gates, measurements, and high-rate code constructions.
motivation: To extend fault-tolerant quantum computing techniques to fermionic systems, specifically Majorana-based qubits, which are a promising platform for topological quantum computation.
method: Generalization of qubit error correction and fault-tolerant protocols to fermionic processes, including design of gates, measurements, and code constructions.
result: Creation of fault-tolerant protocols tailored to Majorana-based codes, enabling universal gates, efficient measurements, and high-rate code constructions.
conclusion: The work provides a foundation for fault-tolerant quantum computing with Majorana qubits, with implications for topological quantum computing and error correction.

title: High-Threshold, Low-Overhead And Single-Shot Decodable Fault-Tolerant Quantum Memory
authors: Thomas R. Scruby, Timo Hillmann, And Joschka Roffe
abstract:
Author(s): Thomas R. Scruby, Timo Hillmann, and Joschka Roffe

Radial codes, a new class of low-density parity-check codes with strong error correction capabilities, tunable parameters, and small size, are shown to be a promising candidate for near-term quantum devices.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020310] Published Fri Apr 17, 2026.
tldr: Radial codes are introduced as a new class of low-density parity-check codes offering high threshold, low overhead, and single-shot decodable fault-tolerant quantum memory.
motivation: To develop quantum error-correcting codes that are practical for near-term devices by achieving high error thresholds, low resource overhead, and efficient decoding.
method: The authors propose radial codes, a family of LDPC codes with tunable parameters, and analyze their performance using numerical simulations and theoretical bounds.
result: Radial codes exhibit high fault-tolerant thresholds, low overhead compared to surface codes, and support single-shot error correction, making them promising for experimental implementation.
conclusion: Radial codes are a strong candidate for near-term quantum memory and fault-tolerant quantum computing, with potential for further optimization and integration into quantum architectures.

title: Quantum Convolutional Neural Networks Are Effectively Classically Simulable
authors: Pablo Bermejo, Paolo Braccia, Manuel S. Rudolph, Zoë Holmes, Lukasz Cincio, And M. Cerezo
abstract:
Author(s): Pablo Bermejo, Paolo Braccia, Manuel S. Rudolph, Zoë Holmes, Lukasz Cincio, and M. Cerezo

The action of a quantum convolutional neural network, which is a promising architecture for quantum machine learning, can be efficiently simulated by a classical computer.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020304] Published Mon Apr 06, 2026.
tldr: Quantum convolutional neural networks can be efficiently simulated classically, challenging their quantum advantage.
motivation: To determine whether quantum convolutional neural networks (QCNNs) offer a quantum advantage over classical methods.
method: The authors theoretically analyze the computational complexity of QCNNs and demonstrate that their action can be simulated efficiently on a classical computer.
result: QCNNs are effectively classically simulable, meaning they do not provide exponential speedup over classical algorithms.
conclusion: The findings suggest that QCNNs may not be a viable candidate for near-term quantum advantage, and alternative quantum machine learning architectures should be explored.

title: 2d Van Der Waals Magnets: From Fundamental Physics To Applications
authors: Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, And Nuh Gedik
abstract:
Author(s): Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, and Nuh Gedik

Scientific discovery is often described as walking into a dark room and turning on the light. The discovery of 2D magnetism in van der Waals materials in 2016 was one such leap forward, removing one spatial dimension from macroscopic materials. The study of 2D magnets has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena. This review summarizes the current state of knowledge of magnetic phenomena in 2D van der Waals materials. The field encompasses not just the traditional study of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets but also topology, quantum and nonequilibrium dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons and spintronics, and the interaction of magnetism with light, phonons, and electric fields (multiferroics). The field is actively evolving, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology while opening new directions for application.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025003] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: A review of 2D van der Waals magnets covering fundamental physics and applications.
motivation: To summarize the current state of knowledge and recent discoveries in 2D magnetism since its experimental realization in 2016.
method: Review article summarizing experimental and theoretical progress in 2D van der Waals magnetic materials.
result: The field encompasses ferromagnets, antiferromagnets, topology, quantum dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons, spintronics, and magneto-optical phenomena.
conclusion: The field is rapidly evolving, expanding theoretical understanding and opening new application directions.

title: Radiation Forces And Torques In Optics And Acoustics
authors: Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, And Konstantin Y. Bliokh
abstract:
Author(s): Ivan Toftul, Sebastian Golat, Francisco J. Rodríguez-Fortuño, Franco Nori, Yuri Kivshar, and Konstantin Y. Bliokh

This review presents a unified perspective of how local energy, momentum, and spin densities in optical and acoustic wave fields induce forces and torques on particles—a topic that has captivated researchers for centuries. Applications discussed include trapping and manipulation of atoms and nanoparticles by light, sorting of biological cells by the combination of acoustics and microfluidics, and pulling forces that draw particles against the direction of wave propagation.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025002] Published Thu Apr 30, 2026.
tldr: This review unifies the description of radiation forces and torques in optics and acoustics, focusing on local energy, momentum, and spin densities.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of how wave fields exert forces and torques on particles, a topic with applications in trapping, manipulation, and sorting.
method: The paper is a review that synthesizes theoretical and experimental results from optics and acoustics, presenting a unified perspective based on local densities.
result: It covers applications such as optical trapping, acoustic sorting, and pulling forces, and highlights the role of spin and momentum densities.
conclusion: The review serves as a reference for researchers in wave-matter interactions, but does not directly address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Exactly Solvable Quantum Many-body Dynamics From Space-time Duality
authors: Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, And Tomaž Prosen
abstract:
Author(s): Bruno Bertini, Pieter W. Claeys, and Tomaž Prosen

Computing quantum dynamics in many-body systems is notoriously difficult. In the past decade, there has been a fundamental advance based on discretizing the time evolution of lattice systems, by analogy with digital computation. Since space is already discrete on a lattice, treating space and time on the same footing avoids the mathematical complications of continuous space-time quantum field theories. This review focuses on how this space-time duality plays out in the dynamics of interacting many-body systems and the intrinsic relationship with special kinds of lattices termed brickwork quantum circuits. From this pedagogical review, readers will learn how this far-reaching analogy with quantum computation lies at the heart of a unified view of dynamical evolution of quantum many-body systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025001] Published Wed Apr 15, 2026.
tldr: This review discusses space-time duality in quantum many-body dynamics using brickwork quantum circuits, focusing on exactly solvable models.
motivation: To provide a pedagogical overview of how space-time duality and quantum circuit analogies can simplify the computation of quantum many-body dynamics.
method: Review of theoretical developments in space-time duality, brickwork quantum circuits, and their application to interacting many-body systems.
result: The paper synthesizes recent advances showing that space-time duality leads to exactly solvable dynamics in certain lattice models.
conclusion: Space-time duality offers a unified framework for understanding quantum many-body dynamics, with potential for further exploration in quantum simulation and computation.

title: Kagome Metals
authors: Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, And Stephen D. Wilson
abstract:
Author(s): Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, and Stephen D. Wilson

The kagome lattice is a two-dimensional tiling of hexagons and triangles named after a Japanese basket weaving technique. Its geometry gives rise to highly frustrated interactions and interference effects experienced by electrons and their multiple degrees of freedom. In metals, the exploration of materials with kagome conduction networks is driven by predictions of realizing new electronic states where these interference effects are dominant, amplifying electronic interactions and many-body effects. In these kagome metals, these amplified correlation effects in combination with spin-orbit coupling and other forms of frustration have given rise to a wealth of phenomena beyond expectations. These include unusual states and responses born from topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, sublattice interference effects at saddle points such as unconventional superconductivity, orbital antiferromagnetism and flux phases, amplified anomalous Hall effects, and electronic nematic states. This review examines the theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, with the aim of elucidating fundamental mechanisms underlying the observed exotic phenomena.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015002] Published Thu Feb 12, 2026.
tldr: This review covers exotic electronic states in kagome metals, focusing on topological flat bands, Dirac fermions, and unconventional superconductivity.
motivation: To understand the fundamental mechanisms behind unusual phenomena observed in kagome metals, driven by frustrated geometry and strong correlations.
method: The paper is a review summarizing theoretical predictions and experimental observations on kagome metals.
result: Key findings include unconventional superconductivity, orbital antiferromagnetism, amplified anomalous Hall effects, and electronic nematic states arising from topological flat bands and sublattice interference.
conclusion: Kagome metals provide a platform for exploring correlated topological phases, with implications for future quantum materials research.

title: Field Theories And Quantum Methods For Stochastic Reaction-diffusion Systems
authors: Mauricio J. Del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, And Wout Merbis
abstract:
Author(s): Mauricio J. del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, and Wout Merbis

The exchange of energy and molecules in a living cell, the spread of opinions through a society, and the flow of traffic in a crowded city are very different phenomena, yet they are all examples of complex systems composed of many agents that interact with each other and exchange energy or particles with the environment. These systems can be modeled as stochastic reaction-diffusion systems. In this pedagogical review, the authors apply powerful field-theoretic methods to these systems, unifying diverse approaches under a single framework. The methods are useful for handling chemical systems but also have applications in a wide range of areas such as ecology and epidemiology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015001] Published Thu Jan 22, 2026.
tldr: This pedagogical review applies field-theoretic methods to stochastic reaction-diffusion systems, unifying diverse approaches for modeling complex systems in chemistry, ecology, and epidemiology.
motivation: To provide a unified framework for stochastic reaction-diffusion systems using field-theoretic methods, which are powerful but often scattered across different disciplines.
method: The authors review and apply field-theoretic techniques, such as path integrals and Doi-Peliti formalism, to stochastic reaction-diffusion models.
result: They demonstrate how these methods unify various approaches and can be applied to a wide range of complex systems beyond chemistry, including ecology and epidemiology.
conclusion: The review highlights the versatility of field-theoretic methods for stochastic systems and suggests further applications in interdisciplinary fields.

title: Spin-glass Dynamics: Experiment, Theory, And Simulation
authors: E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, And D. Yllanes
abstract:
Author(s): E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, and D. Yllanes

This review updates the field of spin glasses with broad application to a large variety of physical systems. In particular, this review tracks the progress of experiment, theory, and large-scale simulations. It highlights the importance of their synergy, from the inception of the field to the present day, and includes future opportunities for research.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045005] Published Mon Dec 15, 2025.
tldr: This review updates the field of spin glasses, covering experiment, theory, and large-scale simulations, with emphasis on their synergy.
motivation: Spin glasses are a model system for complex disordered systems, and the field has progressed significantly; this review aims to consolidate recent advances.
method: The paper is a review that synthesizes experimental results, theoretical developments, and large-scale numerical simulations.
result: The review highlights the interplay between experiment, theory, and simulation, and identifies open questions and future research opportunities.
conclusion: The synergy between different approaches is crucial for progress in spin-glass research, and the field continues to offer challenges and applications to other physical systems.

title: Kitaev Quantum Spin Liquids
authors: Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, And Hae-Young Kee
abstract:
Author(s): Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, and Hae-Young Kee

Frustration in spin systems can prevent ordering even at =0, creating quantum spin liquids that have been sought since Anderson’s pioneering work in 1973 and his influential 1987 paper connecting them to high-temperature superconductivity. Kitaev’s solvable spin-1/2 models on a honeycomb lattice brought renewed attention to this field, with Jackeli and Khaliullin later revealing how to engineer Kitaev interactions in real materials. This review highlights theoretical and experimental developments in Kitaev spin liquids, emphasizing leading candidate materials and their broad topological properties such as chiral edge modes. Consequently, it provides essential insights for both experimentalists and theorists working on quantum spin liquid problems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045003] Published Wed Dec 03, 2025.
tldr: This review covers theoretical and experimental progress in Kitaev quantum spin liquids, focusing on candidate materials and topological properties.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of Kitaev spin liquids, a topic of intense interest in condensed matter physics, and to highlight key developments in theory and experiment.
method: Review article summarizing theoretical models (Kitaev honeycomb model) and experimental realizations in materials like α-RuCl3, with discussion of topological properties.
result: The review outlines the current understanding of Kitaev spin liquids, including chiral edge modes and fractionalized excitations, and identifies leading candidate materials.
conclusion: Kitaev spin liquids remain a vibrant field with many open questions; future work may focus on confirming topological order and exploring applications.

title: Statistical Mechanics For Networks Of Real Neurons
authors: Leenoy Meshulam And William Bialek
abstract:
Author(s): Leenoy Meshulam and William Bialek

Our ability to perceive, think, or act relies on coordinated activity in large networks of neurons in the brain. This review examines recent progress in connecting ideas from statistical physics, such as maximum entropy methods and the renormalization group, to quantitative experiments that record the electrical activity of thousands of neurons simultaneously. This quantitative bridge between the new data and statistical physics models uncovers new, quantitatively reproducible behaviors and makes clear that abstract theoretical principles in studies of the brain can have the level of predictive power that we expect in other areas of physics.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045002] Published Thu Nov 06, 2025.
tldr: This review applies statistical physics methods like maximum entropy and renormalization group to analyze large-scale neural recordings, but does not address quantum systems or information thermodynamics.
motivation: To understand how coordinated neural activity in the brain can be described using principles from statistical physics.
method: Review of recent experiments recording electrical activity from thousands of neurons, analyzed with maximum entropy models and renormalization group techniques.
result: Statistical physics models can quantitatively reproduce neural activity patterns and reveal reproducible behaviors.
conclusion: Abstract theoretical principles from physics can achieve predictive power in neuroscience, similar to other areas of physics.

title: The Ups And Downs Of Internal Conversion
authors: Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, And Salvy P. Russo
abstract:
Author(s): Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, and Salvy P. Russo

This review examines the theoretical methods used to describe the photophysical process of internal conversion in quantum systems. These models explore all facets of the nonradiative mechanism, and the review presents an outlook on how they can be incorporated in studies relevant to applications, for example, in photonics and energy harvesting.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035003] Published Tue Sep 16, 2025.
tldr: This review covers theoretical methods for internal conversion in quantum systems, focusing on nonradiative transitions and their applications in photonics and energy harvesting.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of theoretical models describing internal conversion, a key photophysical process, and to highlight how these models can be applied in technologies like photonics and energy harvesting.
method: The paper is a review that surveys various theoretical approaches, likely including quantum dynamics, rate theories, and computational methods, to model internal conversion.
result: The review summarizes the current state of theoretical methods for internal conversion and discusses their integration into application-oriented studies.
conclusion: The authors present an outlook on incorporating these models into practical applications, but the paper does not introduce new results or directly address the user's specific research interests.

title: Photoinduced Nonequilibrium States In Mott Insulators
authors: Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, And Philipp Werner
abstract:
Author(s): Yuta Murakami, Denis Golež, Martin Eckstein, and Philipp Werner

The interplay between nonequilibrium physics and strong electronic correlations offers a unique platform for manipulating material properties, exploring novel optical responses, and uncovering quantum metastable phases. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in understanding the nonequilibrium dynamics of photoexcited Mott insulators—systems where strong interactions and a robust energy gap can give rise to rich and controllable phenomena. We discuss various nonlinear and nonperturbative pathways for driving and controlling Mott insulators using strong static or periodic fields. Furthermore, the review highlights key mechanisms that govern the evolution of photodoped carriers and the emergence of metastable and nonthermal states characterized by superconducting, magnetic, orbital, and excitonic orders.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035001] Published Thu Jul 31, 2025.
tldr: A review of nonequilibrium dynamics in photoexcited Mott insulators, focusing on strong correlations and photoinduced phase transitions.
motivation: To understand and control material properties using light in strongly correlated systems, exploring novel optical responses and metastable phases.
method: Comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental advances, discussing nonlinear and nonperturbative driving pathways.
result: Key mechanisms for photodoped carrier evolution and emergence of metastable orders (superconducting, magnetic, etc.) are highlighted.
conclusion: Provides a framework for future research in nonequilibrium strongly correlated systems, with potential for material control and quantum metastable phases.

title: Colloquium: Quantum Properties And Functionalities Of Magnetic Skyrmions
authors: Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, And Christos Panagopoulos
abstract:
Author(s): Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, and Christos Panagopoulos

Skyrmions are topological field configurations that were first discussed in the context of high-energy theory. In recent years, skyrmionic spin patterns in solid-state systems have received much attention, in part for their promising application potential. This Colloquium discusses quantum-mechanical aspects of such magnetic skyrmions, both for the interactions that underlie skyrmion formation and for quantum features of the skyrmions themselves.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 031001] Published Tue Jul 08, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews quantum-mechanical aspects of magnetic skyrmions, including their formation interactions and intrinsic quantum features.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of quantum properties of magnetic skyrmions, which have been studied mainly classically, and to highlight their potential for quantum technologies.
method: Review article summarizing theoretical and experimental progress on quantum skyrmions, covering interactions, dynamics, and quantum coherence.
result: Discusses quantum effects in skyrmion formation, such as quantum fluctuations and topological protection, and explores skyrmions as candidates for qubits or quantum information carriers.
conclusion: Quantum skyrmions offer a new platform for exploring topological quantum phenomena and may enable future quantum devices, but many challenges remain in observing and controlling quantum coherence.

title: Spin-dependent Exotic Interactions
authors: Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, And Dmitry Budker
abstract:
Author(s): Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, and Dmitry Budker

This review presents a comprehensive summary of theoretical investigations and experimental searches for spin-dependent interactions beyond the standard model. These interactions may be mediated by various types of exotic bosons, and their existence and properties may, in turn, explain the nature of dark matter and dark energy. The described experiments also probe the discrete fundamental symmetries of nature.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025005] Published Tue Jun 24, 2025.
tldr: A comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental searches for spin-dependent exotic interactions beyond the Standard Model, including their possible role in dark matter and dark energy.
motivation: To systematically survey the landscape of spin-dependent forces mediated by exotic bosons, which could reveal new physics beyond the Standard Model and shed light on dark matter and dark energy.
method: The paper is a review that compiles theoretical models (e.g., axion-mediated interactions, spin-spin couplings) and experimental constraints from precision measurements, atomic physics, and astrophysical observations.
result: The review catalogs various exotic spin-dependent interactions and the current experimental bounds, highlighting the most sensitive probes and remaining parameter space.
conclusion: Spin-dependent exotic interactions remain a promising avenue for discovering new physics, and future experiments with improved sensitivity could detect or further constrain these interactions.

title: Colloquium: Qudits For Decomposing Multiqubit Gates And Realizing Quantum Algorithms
authors: Evgeniy O. Kiktenko, Anastasiia S. Nikolaeva, And Aleksey K. Fedorov
abstract:
Author(s): Evgeniy O. Kiktenko, Anastasiia S. Nikolaeva, and Aleksey K. Fedorov

Two-level systems—bits or qubits—are understood to generally be the most efficient primitives for information processing, classical or quantum. But this is not to say that there are no roles to be played by multilevel systems. This Colloquium surveys these possible roles for the quantum case. Here we speak of qudits:
[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021003] Published Tue Jun 03, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews the use of qudits (multilevel quantum systems) for decomposing multiqubit gates and implementing quantum algorithms, highlighting potential simplifications like the Toffoli gate with a qutrit.
motivation: To survey the roles of qudits in quantum computing, challenging the assumption that qubits are always optimal, and to explore practical advantages in gate decomposition and algorithm realization.
method: Review of theoretical proposals and experimental implementations of qudit-based quantum computing, including qudit-qubit embeddings and gate decompositions.
result: Qudits can simplify certain multiqubit gates (e.g., Toffoli gate with a qutrit) and offer resource-efficient implementations, but experimental progress is still limited.
conclusion: Qudits provide a promising alternative for specific quantum computing tasks, but further experimental development is needed to realize their potential.

title: Colloquium: Materials That Exceed Classical Thermodynamic Bounds On Properties
authors: Roderic S. Lakes
abstract:
Author(s): Roderic S. Lakes

Classical thermodynamic bounds provide constraints on values that are expected in measurements of certain physical properties. In a variety of fields, some measurements exceed these bounds. This apparent violation of thermodynamics arises because the measurements are made in ways that violate the underlying assumptions made when deriving these bounds. This Colloquium describes a wide variety of circumstances where such violations occur and which of the underlying assumptions are violated in each case. It also describes how interesting material properties can be developed using materials designed to violate these assumptions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021002] Published Wed May 14, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews materials that appear to exceed classical thermodynamic bounds on properties, explaining how violations arise from measurement conditions that break underlying assumptions.
motivation: To clarify why some measurements of material properties exceed classical thermodynamic bounds and to explore how these violations can be exploited to develop materials with enhanced properties.
method: The paper surveys a wide variety of experimental and theoretical examples where bounds are exceeded, analyzing which assumptions (e.g., equilibrium, linearity, homogeneity) are violated in each case.
result: Many apparent violations are due to measurements made under non-equilibrium conditions, with inhomogeneous materials, or with active external driving, rather than actual violations of thermodynamics.
conclusion: Understanding the assumptions behind thermodynamic bounds allows the design of materials that circumvent these bounds for practical applications, but no fundamental thermodynamic principles are violated.

title: Codata Recommended Values Of The Fundamental Physical Constants: 2022
authors: Peter J. Mohr, David B. Newell, Barry N. Taylor, And Eite Tiesinga
abstract:
Author(s): Peter J. Mohr, David B. Newell, Barry N. Taylor, and Eite Tiesinga

This review contains the 2022 self-consistent set of values of the constants and conversion factors of physics and chemistry recommended by the Committee on Data for Science and Technology (CODATA). The CODATA values are based on a least-squares adjustment that takes into account all data available up to the end of 2022. Details of the data selection and methodology are described.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025002] Published Wed Apr 30, 2025.
tldr: This paper presents the 2022 CODATA recommended values of fundamental physical constants based on a least-squares adjustment of all available data up to the end of 2022.
motivation: To provide an updated, self-consistent set of fundamental constants for use in science and technology.
method: Least-squares adjustment of experimental and theoretical data from various sources.
result: New recommended values for fundamental constants and conversion factors.
conclusion: The updated constants are essential for precision measurements and theoretical calculations across physics and chemistry.

title: Colloquium: Synthetic Quantum Matter In Nonstandard Geometries
authors: Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, And Christof Weitenberg
abstract:
Author(s): Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, and Christof Weitenberg

This Colloquium presents ways to implement fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems. The study of quantum many-body physics in these exotic geometries permits simulation of phenomena from topology in condensed matter to models of gravity and cosmology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 011001] Published Tue Mar 25, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews experimental and theoretical progress in realizing quantum many-body systems on fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions using atomic, photonic, and electronic platforms.
motivation: To explore quantum many-body physics in nonstandard geometries that are not naturally available, enabling simulation of phenomena from condensed matter topology to gravity and cosmology.
method: The paper surveys multiple experimental platforms (ultracold atoms, photonic systems, electronic materials) and theoretical approaches for implementing fractal, curved, and higher-dimensional geometries.
result: Key results include demonstrations of topological states in fractal lattices, quantum simulators of curved spaces, and synthetic dimensions that mimic higher-dimensional physics.
conclusion: These synthetic quantum matter platforms open new avenues for studying exotic quantum phenomena and may lead to insights into fundamental physics, though many challenges remain in scaling and control.

title: Massive Quantum Systems As Interfaces Of Quantum Mechanics And Gravity
authors: Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, And Clara C. Wanjura
abstract:
Author(s): Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, and Clara C. Wanjura

The authors review theories and experimental state-of-the-art efforts to study the effects of gravity on massive quantum systems. Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force and may be addressed via precision quantum probes. Experiments testing whether the quantum nature of gravity causes decoherence and collapse of matter-wave functions and whether it can mediate entanglement between separate massive particles are underway, and their results will guide the theoretical description of gravity effects on a laboratory scale.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015003] Published Thu Feb 13, 2025.
tldr: This review explores the intersection of quantum mechanics and gravity using massive quantum systems, focusing on experimental tests of gravity's quantum effects.
motivation: To understand how gravity affects massive quantum systems and to test whether gravity is fundamentally quantum, which could guide the development of a quantum theory of gravity.
method: The paper reviews theoretical frameworks (e.g., decoherence models, entanglement mediation) and experimental approaches (e.g., matter-wave interferometry, optomechanics) for probing gravity with massive quantum systems.
result: The authors summarize current theoretical proposals and experimental efforts, noting that experiments testing gravity-induced decoherence and entanglement are underway but have not yet reached conclusive results.
conclusion: Massive quantum systems offer a promising avenue to test quantum gravity effects, but further theoretical and experimental advances are needed to distinguish between classical and quantum gravity.

title: Construction Of near-Γ Multiple Chiral Exceptional Points In Momentum Space Of Photonic Crystal Slabs
authors: Jingyu Zhang, Yang Gao, Tianfu Ma, Wenjia Li, Weimin Ye And Jianlong Liu
abstract: Exceptional points (EPs) in optical systems have attracted considerable attention because of their nontrivial topological properties and unusual physical effects. Among them, scattering EPs are particularly appealing for describing chiral response through the scattering matrix. Photonic crystal slabs offer a versatile platform for studying chiral scattering EPs in momentum space, where their topological evolution can be conveniently accessed and engineered. In this work, a convenient approach is presented for achieving chiral scattering EPs near the Γ point by exploiting the topological evolution properties in the momentum space of photonic crystal slabs. By varying the structural parameters of the photonic crystal slabs, multiple chiral EPs are identified near the Γ point, with their evolution and annihilation processes systematically analyzed. Furthermore, the pronounced transmission asymmetry observed near the EP enables polarization conversion from linear to circular, functioning as a quarter-wave plate. This approach provides a straightforward method for realizing and controlling chiral EPs in momentum space, thereby expanding the potential for practical applications in optical metadevices.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a method to create multiple chiral exceptional points near the Γ point in photonic crystal slabs, enabling polarization conversion.
motivation: Exceptional points in optical systems have unique topological properties; the goal is to achieve and control chiral scattering EPs in momentum space for practical applications.
method: The authors vary structural parameters of photonic crystal slabs and analyze topological evolution in momentum space to identify chiral EPs near the Γ point.
result: Multiple chiral EPs are identified, their evolution and annihilation are analyzed, and transmission asymmetry near the EP enables linear-to-circular polarization conversion.
conclusion: This approach provides a straightforward method for realizing and controlling chiral EPs, expanding potential for optical metadevices.

title: Integrated Error-suppressed Pipeline For Quantum Optimization Of Nontrivial Binary Combinatorial Optimization Problems On Gate-model Hardware At The 156-qubit Scale
authors: Natasha Sachdeva, Gavin S Hartnett, Smarak Maity, Samuel Marsh, Yulun Wang, Adam Winick, Ryan Dougherty, Daniel Canuto, You Quan Chong, G Adam Cox, Michael Hush, Pranav S Mundada, Christopher D B Bentley, Michael J Biercuk And Yuval Baum
abstract: We introduce a novel hybrid quantum–classical variational optimization method for unconstrained binary combinatorial optimization problems on gate-model quantum computers, integrating a custom variational ansatz, staged feedback-based dual variational parameter update strategies, efficient parametric compilation, automated error suppression during hardware execution, and scalable O( ) classical post-processing to correct for bitflip errors. Without this integrated approach, we show that standard circuit execution at scale produces output indistinguishable from random sampling, establishing the necessity of each pipeline component. We benchmark the method on IBM superconducting quantum computers for several optimization problems drawn from NP-hard problem classes, where the optimization is conducted on hardware with no use of classical simulation or prior knowledge of the solution. For Max-Cut on random regular graphs with topologies not matched to device connectivity, the method achieves approximation ratios (AR) of 100% for unweighted 3-regular graphs up to 156 nodes, weighted regular graphs up to 80 nodes, and weighted 7-regular graphs up 50 nodes. Applied to higher-order binary optimization, the method finds the ground state energy of 127- and 156-qubit spin-glass models matched to device topology with linear, quadratic, and cubic interaction terms, achieving ARs of at least 99.5% across all instances tested. The method consistently outperforms a classical local solver across all problems. Where published results on identical problem instances are available, our method demonstrates competitive or superior performance. These results demonstrate that an appropriately engineered variational approach enables gate-model quantum computers to produce high-quality solutions for binary optimization problems drawn from NP-hard problem classes at the 156-qubit scale, where naïve implementations are insufficient for good performance.
tldr: This paper presents a hybrid quantum-classical variational optimization pipeline for binary combinatorial problems on gate-model quantum computers, achieving high approximation ratios on up to 156 qubits.
motivation: To demonstrate that gate-model quantum computers can solve NP-hard binary optimization problems at scale with an integrated error-suppressed pipeline, overcoming the limitations of naive implementations.
method: The method combines a custom variational ansatz, staged feedback-based dual variational parameter updates, efficient parametric compilation, automated error suppression, and scalable classical post-processing for bitflip error correction.
result: The pipeline achieves 100% approximation ratios for Max-Cut on unweighted 3-regular graphs up to 156 nodes and at least 99.5% for spin-glass models up to 156 qubits, outperforming classical local solvers.
conclusion: The integrated approach enables gate-model quantum computers to produce high-quality solutions for binary optimization problems at the 156-qubit scale, suggesting that variational methods with error suppression are viable for near-term quantum advantage.

title: Geometry-resolved Suppression Of Patch-potential Heating In Skeleton-electrode Ion Traps
authors: Chon-Teng Belmiro Chu, Hao-Chung Chen, Ting Hsu, Hsiang-Yu Lo, Ming-Shien Chang And Guin-Dar Lin
abstract: We present a quantitative, geometry-resolved framework to evaluate the effects of patch-potential noise in realistic three-dimensional Paul-trap structures. As a concrete application, we analyze a skeleton-electrode architecture and compare its performance against a conventional blade trap under identical ion-to-electrode distances and matched confinement parameters. The skeleton geometry achieves a suppression of motional heating exceeding 50%, with heating rate ratios of for the axial mode and for the radial mode. Patch-by-patch heating maps reveal that over 99% of the noise contribution originates from electrode surfaces within 500 m of the ion. We identify that axial heating follows a non-monotonic profile, with dominant ‘hotspots’ located at an intermediate distance of approximately 110 m. This behavior is driven by the vectorial directionality of the electric-field components, which provide the strongest axial coupling at these intermediate regions. Guided by these maps, we demonstrate a proof-of-principle electrode reconfiguration where segmented gaps are aligned with identified hotspots. This strategy successfully reduces axial heating even when the total electrode surface area increases, confirming that the spatial distribution of noise coupling—rather than total conductor area—is the primary driver of motional heating. These findings establish geometry-guided design as a practical route to suppress heating in trapped-ion platform, and the proposed skeleton architecture is compatible with advanced fabrication techniques, including metal additive manufacturing.
tldr: This paper presents a geometry-resolved framework to evaluate patch-potential heating in ion traps, demonstrating that skeleton-electrode designs can suppress motional heating by over 50% compared to conventional blade traps.
motivation: Motional heating from patch potentials is a major decoherence source in trapped-ion quantum computing. The authors aimed to understand how electrode geometry influences heating and to design traps with reduced noise.
method: They developed a quantitative framework to compute patch-potential noise in realistic 3D Paul traps, applied it to a skeleton-electrode architecture and a conventional blade trap, and generated patch-by-patch heating maps to identify noise hotspots.
result: The skeleton geometry suppresses heating by >50% for both axial and radial modes. Over 99% of noise comes from electrodes within 500 μm of the ion, and axial heating has a non-monotonic profile with hotspots at ~110 μm. Reconfiguring electrode gaps to align with hotspots reduces heating even with increased surface area.
conclusion: Geometry-guided design is a practical route to suppress heating in ion traps, and the skeleton architecture is compatible with advanced fabrication like metal additive manufacturing.

title: Probing A Theoretical Framework For A Photonic Extreme Learning Machine
authors: Vicente Rocha, Duarte Silva, Felipe C Moreira, Catarina S Monteiro, Tiago D Ferreira And Nuno A Silva
abstract: The development of computing paradigms alternative to von Neumann architectures has recently fueled significant progress in novel all-optical processing solutions. In this work, we investigate how the coherence properties can be exploited for computing by expanding information onto a higher-dimensional space in the photonic extreme learning machine framework. A theoretical framework is provided based on the transmission matrix formalism, mapping the input plane onto the output camera plane, resulting in the establishment of the connection with complex extreme learning machines and derivation of upper bounds for the hidden space dimensionality as well as the form of the activation functions. Experiments using free-space propagation through a diffusive medium, performed in low-dimensional input space regimes, validate the model and the proposed estimator for the dimensionality. Overall, the framework presented and the findings enclosed have the potential to foster further research in a multitude of directions, from the development of robust general-purpose all-optical hardware to a full-stack integration with optical sensing devices toward edge computing solutions.
tldr: This paper presents a theoretical framework for a photonic extreme learning machine using free-space propagation through a diffusive medium, focusing on coherence properties and dimensionality expansion.
motivation: To develop alternative computing paradigms beyond von Neumann architectures by exploiting optical coherence for all-optical processing.
method: The authors use a transmission matrix formalism to map input to output planes, derive upper bounds for hidden space dimensionality, and validate with experiments using free-space propagation through a diffusive medium.
result: The model establishes a connection with complex extreme learning machines and provides an estimator for dimensionality, validated in low-dimensional input regimes.
conclusion: The framework may foster research in all-optical hardware and edge computing, but its direct relevance to the user's interests in quantum information thermodynamics, foundations, communication, or hybrid quantum systems is minimal.

title: Emergent Hydrodynamics Of Chiral Active Fluids: Vortices, Bubbles And Odd Diffusion
authors: Umberto Marini Bettolo Marconi, Alessandro Petrini, Raphael Maire And Lorenzo Caprini
abstract: Starting from a microscopic multiparticle Langevin equation, we obtain a hydrodynamic description in terms of density and momentum fields for chiral active particles interacting via standard repulsive and nonlocal odd forces. These odd interactions are reciprocal but non-conservative: they are non-potential forces, as they act perpendicular to the vector joining any pair of particles. As a result, the torques that two particles exert on one another are non-reciprocal. The ensuing macroscopic continuum description consists of a continuity equation for the density and a generalized compressible Navier–Stokes equation for the fluid velocity. The latter includes a chirality-induced torque density term and an odd viscosity contribution. Our theory predicts the emergence of odd diffusivity, edge currents, and is consistent with an inhomogeneous phase—characterized by bubble-like structures—recently observed in simulations. Specifically, the theory exhibits a linear instability arising from the interplay between odd viscosity and torque density, and admits steady-state inhomogeneous solutions featuring bubbles and vortices, in qualitative agreement with numerical simulations. Our findings can be tested experimentally in systems of granular spinners or rotating microorganisms suspended in a fluid.
tldr: This paper derives a hydrodynamic theory for chiral active fluids with odd interactions, predicting odd diffusion, edge currents, and bubble-like phases.
motivation: To understand the collective behavior of chiral active particles (e.g., granular spinners, rotating microorganisms) where interactions are non-conservative and lead to novel emergent phenomena.
method: Starting from a microscopic multiparticle Langevin equation with repulsive and odd forces, the authors derive macroscopic continuity and Navier-Stokes equations using standard coarse-graining techniques.
result: The theory reveals odd viscosity, odd diffusivity, and a linear instability that produces steady-state inhomogeneous solutions (bubbles and vortices), matching simulations.
conclusion: The findings provide a theoretical framework for chiral active fluids and can be tested in experiments with granular spinners or rotating microorganisms.

title: Probing Electron Correlations In Solids With Auger-photoelectron Coincidence Spectroscopy
authors: Roberto Gotter And Giovanni Stefani Robert A Bartynski
abstract: Auger photoelectron coincidence spectroscopy (APECS) has emerged as a powerful tool for probing electron–electron correlation in solids. When a photoexcited core hole decays via a core-valence-valence Auger transition, two valence holes are created in the final state. Consequently, the line shape of the Auger electron spectrum is influenced by both Coulomb and exchange interactions between the two holes. By simultaneously detecting the photoelectron and Auger electron emitted from a single photoionization event, APECS measurements place constraints on the two final state holes, enabling one to independently measure Coulomb and exchange correlation energies. This review highlights the key advantages of APECS over other electron spectroscopic techniques including separating overlapping spectral features, removing the background signal from inelastically scattered electrons, enhanced surface sensitivity and site specificity. It also cites examples of how these attributes can be used to investigate the properties of solids in an unprecedented manner. To aid in understanding APECS data and assist in experimental design, a phenomenological model for the probability of electron pair emission as a function of the photo- and Auger electron kinetic energies and emission angles is presented. The model is applied to a hypothetical solid, demonstrating how the contribution to APECS spectrum of final states with different spin configurations depends on these experimental parameters. A summary of results obtained by performing one-dimensional (as a function of Auger [EA] or photoelectron [EP] kinetic energy), two-dimensional (parallel detection of EAand EP) and angle-resolved (AR) (as a function of EA at specific photo- and Auger electron emission angles) APECS measurements is presented. In particular, measurements of ferromagnetic metals and antiferromagnetic transition metal oxides demonstrate how AR-APECS is a powerful tool for independently measuring Coulomb and exchange correlation energies. Finally, potential future applications of APECS and further developments of this experimental technique are discussed.
tldr: This paper reviews Auger-photoelectron coincidence spectroscopy (APECS) as a technique to probe electron correlations in solids, focusing on Coulomb and exchange interactions in valence holes.
motivation: To demonstrate the advantages of APECS over conventional electron spectroscopies for studying electron-electron correlations in solids, particularly in ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic materials.
method: The paper presents a phenomenological model for electron pair emission probability and reviews one-dimensional, two-dimensional, and angle-resolved APECS measurements.
result: APECS can separate overlapping spectral features, remove inelastic background, and independently measure Coulomb and exchange correlation energies, as shown in studies of ferromagnetic metals and antiferromagnetic oxides.
conclusion: APECS is a powerful tool for investigating electron correlations, with potential future applications in complex materials and further technique developments.

title: Observation Of Custodial Chiral Symmetry In Memristive Topological Circuits
authors: Wenhao Li, Junyao Wu, Ning Han, Rui Zhao, Fujia Chen, Yuang Pan, Yudong Ren, Hongsheng Chen, Zhen Gao, Ce Shang And Yihao Yang
abstract: The concept of custodial symmetry, a residual symmetry that protects physical observables from large quantum corrections, has been a cornerstone of high-energy physics. In classical engineered systems, however, experimental realization and observation of its classical analog have remained unexplored. Building on recent theoretical work (2022 Phys. Rev. Lett.128 097701), we report the first experimental observation of a classical analog of custodial chiral symmetry in a memristive Su–Schrieffer–Heeger (SSH) circuit. We provide direct experimental evidence for custodial symmetry by measuring the correction to the Lagrangian. This Lagrangian correction, which mimics a mass term in field theory, vanishes smoothly as the perturbation is reduced. We also demonstrate that topological edge states in the memristive SSH circuit remain localized at the boundary, consistent with custodial chiral symmetry. This work opens new avenues for emulating field-theoretic symmetries and nonlinear dynamics in memristive platforms.
tldr: This paper reports the first experimental observation of a classical analog of custodial chiral symmetry in a memristive topological circuit, demonstrating that topological edge states remain localized under perturbations.
motivation: To experimentally realize and observe a classical analog of custodial chiral symmetry, a concept from high-energy physics, in an engineered classical system.
method: The authors built a memristive Su–Schrieffer–Heeger (SSH) circuit and measured the Lagrangian correction as a function of perturbation strength, providing direct evidence for custodial symmetry.
result: The Lagrangian correction vanishes smoothly as perturbation is reduced, and topological edge states remain localized, consistent with custodial chiral symmetry.
conclusion: This work opens new avenues for emulating field-theoretic symmetries and nonlinear dynamics in memristive platforms, but has limited direct connection to the user's research interests.

title: 2d Excitonics With Atomically Thin Lateral Heterostructures
authors: S Shradha, R Rosati, H Lamsaadi, J Picker, I Paradisanos, Md T Hossain, L Krelle, L F Oswald, N Engel, D I Markina, K Watanabe, T Taniguchi, P K Sahoo, L Lombez, X Marie, P Renucci, V Paillard, J-M Poumirol, A Turchanin, E Malic And B Urbaszek
abstract: Semiconducting transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs), such as MoSe2 and WSe2, exhibit unique optical and electronic properties. Vertical stacking of layers of one or more TMDs, to create heterostructures, has expanded the fields of moiré physics and twistronics. Bottom-up fabrication techniques, such as chemical vapor deposition, have advanced the creation of heterostructures beyond what was possible with mechanical exfoliation and stacking. These techniques now enable the fabrication of lateral heterostructures (LHs), where two or more monolayers are covalently bonded in the plane of their atoms. At their atomically sharp interfaces, lateral heterostructures exhibit additional phenomena, such as the formation of charge-transfer excitons, in which the electron and hole reside on opposite sides of the interface. Due to the energy landscape created by differences in the band structures of the constituent materials, unique effects such as unidirectional exciton transport and excitonic lensing can be observed in LHs. This review outlines recent progress in exciton dynamics and spectroscopy of TMD-based LHs and offers an outlook on future developments in excitonics in this promising system.
tldr: This review summarizes recent progress in exciton dynamics and spectroscopy of atomically thin lateral heterostructures of transition metal dichalcogenides.
motivation: To provide an overview of the emerging field of 2D excitonics based on lateral heterostructures, highlighting unique phenomena such as charge-transfer excitons and unidirectional exciton transport.
method: The paper is a review that compiles and discusses recent experimental and theoretical results on TMD lateral heterostructures, focusing on exciton dynamics and spectroscopy.
result: Key findings include the formation of charge-transfer excitons at atomically sharp interfaces, unidirectional exciton transport, and excitonic lensing effects.
conclusion: Lateral heterostructures offer a promising platform for excitonics with potential applications in optoelectronics, but the paper does not directly address the user's research interests in thermodynamics, quantum foundations, communication, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Fractionalized Fermi Liquids And The Cuprate Phase Diagram
authors: Pietro M Bonetti, Maine Christos, Alexander Nikolaenko, Aavishkar A Patel And Subir Sachdev
abstract: We review a theoretical framework for the cuprate superconductors, rooted in a fractionalized Fermi liquid (FL*) description of the intermediate-temperature pseudogap phase at low doping. The FL* theory predicted hole pockets each of fractional area at hole doping p, in contrast to the area in spin density wave theory. Magnetotransport measurements, including observation of the Yamaji angle, show clear evidence of hole pocket quasiparticles which can tunnel coherently between square lattice layers, and are consistent with the FL* description. The FL* phase of a single-band model is described using a layer construction with a pair of ancilla qubits on each site: the Ancilla layer model (ALM). Its mean field theory yields hole pockets of area , and matches the gapped photoemission spectrum in the anti-nodal region of the Brillouin zone. Fluctuations are described by the SU(2) gauge theory of a background spin liquid with critical Dirac spinons. A Monte Carlo study of the thermal SU(2) gauge theory transforms the hole pockets into Fermi arcs in photoemission. One route to confinement of FL* upon lowering temperature yields a d-wave superconductor via a Kosterlitz–Thouless transition of vortices, with nodal Bogoliubov quasiparticles featuring anisotropic velocities and vortices surrounded by charge order halos. An alternative route yields a charge-ordered metallic state that has quantum oscillations consistent with observations. These confinement transitions are driven by the condensation of a SU(2) fundamental Higgs field, which also provides a fractionalized description of intertwined orders. Increasing doping from the FL* phase in the ALM drives a transition to a conventional FL at large doping, passing through an intermediate strange metal regime. We formulate a theory of the FL*-FL metal-metal transition without a symmetry-breaking order parameter, using a critical quantum ‘charge’ liquid of mobile electrons in the presence of disorder, developed via an extension of the Sachdev–Ye–Kitaev model to two spatial dimensions. At low temperatures, and across optimal and over doping, we address the regimes of extended non-FL behavior by Griffiths effects near quantum phase transitions in disordered metals. Partly based on lectures by S S at Boulder School 2025, Dynamics of Strongly Correlated Electrons, 14–18 July. Lecture videos. Joint ICTP-WE Heraeus School and Workshop on Advances in Quantum Matter: Pushing the Boundaries, ICTP, Trieste, 4, 6 August 2025. Lecture videos. School on Quantum Dynamics of Matter, Light and Information, ICTP, Trieste, 18, 19 August 2025. Lecture videos. Croucher Advanced Study Institute for Fractional Chern Insulators, University of Hong Kong, 4, 5 September 2025. Lecture slides. Advanced School and Conference on Quantum Matter, ICTP Trieste, 1–12 December 2025. Lecture Notes. Lecture videos.
tldr: This paper reviews a theoretical framework for cuprate superconductors based on fractionalized Fermi liquids, focusing on the pseudogap phase and phase diagram.
motivation: To explain the intermediate-temperature pseudogap phase in cuprates and the transition to a strange metal and conventional Fermi liquid.
method: Theoretical review using the Ancilla layer model, SU(2) gauge theory, and extensions of the Sachdev–Ye–Kitaev model.
result: The FL* theory predicts hole pockets of fractional area, matches photoemission spectra, and describes confinement transitions to d-wave superconductivity or charge order.
conclusion: The framework provides a unified description of cuprate phases, but experimental validation and further development of the critical quantum charge liquid theory are needed.

tldr: This paper presents a method to generate high-quality electron bunches using a plasma photoinjector with spatiotemporal laser control, aimed at particle collider applications.
motivation: To produce electron bunches with collider-quality parameters (low emittance, high charge) using a compact all-optical plasma-based accelerator, which could reduce the size and cost of future colliders.
method: The approach uses spatiotemporally shaped laser pulses to create a moving ionization front inside a nonlinear plasma wave, trapping and accelerating electrons to produce bunches with controlled properties.
result: Simulations and experiments demonstrate that the moving ionization front can generate electron bunches with normalized emittance below 0.1 mm-mrad and charge of tens of pC, meeting collider requirements.
conclusion: This work shows a viable path to compact plasma-based colliders, but further experimental validation and scaling to higher energies are needed.

authors: Jack Binysh, Guido Baardink, Jonas Veenstra, Corentin Coulais, And Anton Souslov
abstract:
Author(s): Jack Binysh, Guido Baardink, Jonas Veenstra, Corentin Coulais, and Anton Souslov

By combining experiments with robotic metamaterials and theory, this work shows that increasing microscopic activity can counterintuitively cause a solid’s macroscale active response to vanish when active units are too sparse for the active forces to percolate through the structure.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021012] Published Mon Apr 13, 2026.
tldr: Increasing microscopic activity in unpercolated active solids can counterintuitively cause the macroscopic active response to vanish.
motivation: To understand how the spatial arrangement of active units affects the collective mechanical response of active solids, particularly when active units are sparse.
method: Combined experiments with robotic metamaterials and theoretical modeling to study active solids with non-percolating active units.
result: When active units are too sparse to percolate, increasing their activity reduces the overall macroscopic response, a 'more is less' effect.
conclusion: The percolation of active forces is crucial for macroscopic activity; this work highlights the role of network topology in active matter.

motivation: To understand how mechanical forces and flows drive chromatin organization within the nucleus, which is crucial for gene regulation and cellular function.

title: Colloquium: Radio Astronomy With The Arecibo 305-m Telescope: In Contemporaneous Context
authors: Tapasi Ghosh And Chris Salter
abstract:
Author(s): Tapasi Ghosh and Chris Salter

The Arecibo Observatory, inaugurated in 1963 as the world’s largest single-dish radio telescope, remained at the forefront of astronomy and atmospheric science for more than five decades, until its catastrophic collapse in December 2020. This Colloquium focuses on Arecibo’s enduring legacy in radio astronomy, offering a historical perspective that emphasizes how successive major upgrades of the telescope continuously expanded its observational capabilities and scientific impact. It presents Arecibo’s most influential contributions in topics as diverse as pulsar studies, the mapping of neutral hydrogen (HI) in the Milky Way and other galaxies, the characterization of the interstellar medium, the imaging of extragalactic radio sources with very long baseline interferometry (VLBI), the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI), and being a major contributor to the first-ever detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011004] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: A historical review of the Arecibo 305-m telescope's contributions to radio astronomy, from pulsars to gravitational waves.
motivation: To document the scientific legacy of the Arecibo Observatory after its collapse, highlighting its major upgrades and discoveries.
method: Historical narrative and review of key scientific results obtained with the Arecibo telescope over its lifetime.
result: Arecibo made seminal contributions to pulsar studies, HI mapping, VLBI, SETI, and the detection of the stochastic gravitational-wave background.
conclusion: The telescope's unique capabilities enabled breakthroughs that shaped modern radio astronomy; its loss is a major setback for the field.

tldr: This paper reviews the physics and chemistry of transplutonium compounds under high pressure, focusing on their electronic properties and behavior.
