title: Colloquium: Multimessenger Astronomy With Continuous Gravitational Waves And Future Detectors
authors: Benjamin J. Owen
abstract:
Author(s): Benjamin J. Owen

The search for continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars represents a key frontier of gravitational-wave astrophysics, with strong connections to electromagnetic astronomy, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics. This Colloquium discusses the detection prospects for these long-lived yet elusive signals in the upcoming generation of gravitational-wave detectors, emphasizing the importance of simultaneous electromagnetic observations. It also surveys the potential implications of such multimessenger observations for our understanding of the physical and astrophysical processes taking place in the extremely dense environments of their sources.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011002] Published Tue Mar 10, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews the prospects for multimessenger astronomy using continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars and future detectors.
motivation: To discuss detection prospects for continuous gravitational waves and their connection to electromagnetic observations, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics.
method: Review and survey of theoretical and observational prospects for continuous gravitational wave detection with next-generation detectors.
result: The paper outlines the potential for multimessenger observations combining gravitational and electromagnetic signals to study neutron star interiors and dense matter.
conclusion: Continuous gravitational waves offer a new window into neutron star physics, but the paper does not directly address the user's specific research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Colloquium: Gravitational Waves From Neutrino-driven Core Collapse Supernovae
authors: A. Mezzacappa And M. Zanolin
abstract:
Author(s): A. Mezzacappa and M. Zanolin

The observation of a core collapse supernova explosion of (near-)Galactic origin would constitute a landmark, once-in-a-century event for multimessenger astronomy, eagerly awaited by observers and modelers alike. The detection of gravitational waves, along with photons and neutrinos, from such an event would provide unique insights into the supernova central engine and the physics of the newly forming neutron star. This Colloquium presents the latest progress in core collapse supernova modeling and the associated gravitational wave signal predictions. It also provides an overview of the specific methods of detection and physical parameter estimation that can be implemented for such signals in ground-based laser interferometers, in the context of multimessenger research strategies.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041002] Published Tue Dec 30, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews gravitational wave signals from core collapse supernovae and their detection in multimessenger astronomy.
motivation: To summarize progress in modeling core collapse supernovae and predicting gravitational wave signals for upcoming observations.
method: Review of core collapse supernova modeling and gravitational wave signal predictions, along with detection methods for ground-based interferometers.
result: Latest progress in supernova modeling and associated gravitational wave signatures are presented.
conclusion: Detection of gravitational waves from a Galactic supernova would provide unique insights into the supernova engine and neutron star physics.

title: Neutron Stars And The Dense Matter Equation Of State
authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: This review summarizes recent constraints on neutron star masses, radii, and central densities from gravitational-wave and X-ray observations, and compares them to nuclear equation of state calculations.
motivation: To understand the behavior of matter at extreme densities found in neutron stars, which is not accessible in terrestrial experiments.
method: Review of observational data from binary neutron star mergers (gravitational waves) and X-ray pulse profile measurements, compared to theoretical nuclear equation of state models.
result: New constraints on neutron star masses and radii have been obtained, providing insights into the dense matter equation of state.
conclusion: Future observations will further refine the equation of state and may reveal exotic matter phases.

title: Order And Disorder At The Atomic Scale: Microscopy Applied To Semiconductors
authors: Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, And Lorenzo Rigutti
abstract:
Author(s): Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, and Lorenzo Rigutti

Atomic-scale details, especially those of disorder, are important for material properties, especially in semiconductors, but they are also extremely difficult to measure. Real-space methods can give direct access to this information, but typically, that access is limited. This review reports the application of three real-space techniques for measuring disorder to compound semiconductor materials: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy. Where possible, it emphasizes cases in which the probes have been combined to achieve a more complete picture of the defects.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025006] Published Thu Jun 26, 2025.
tldr: This review covers three real-space microscopy techniques for measuring atomic-scale disorder in semiconductors.
motivation: Atomic-scale disorder critically affects semiconductor properties but is difficult to measure; the review aims to showcase how real-space methods can address this challenge.
method: The authors review scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy, emphasizing combined approaches.
result: The paper demonstrates that these techniques can directly reveal atomic-scale disorder and defects in compound semiconductors.
conclusion: Combining multiple real-space probes provides a more complete picture of defects, which is important for understanding and engineering semiconductor materials.

title: Quantum Physics Of Stars
authors: M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. Deboer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, And A. Tumino
abstract:
Author(s): M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. deBoer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, and A. Tumino

There are many nuclear reactions that are of central importance for stellar burning and element formation. In typical stars, these reactions take place at very low energy, and many of them have very small rates, making it difficult to measure them directly in the laboratory. On the theoretical side, the low-energy regime is governed by quantum-mechanical phenomena like tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects. This review summarizes the state of the art in the theory of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars and describes new ideas for studying these reactions on Earth.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025003] Published Tue May 27, 2025.
tldr: A review of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars, focusing on quantum tunneling, resonances, and interference effects.
motivation: To understand nuclear reactions that power stars and synthesize elements, which are difficult to measure directly due to low rates.
method: Review of theoretical approaches including quantum tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects, along with experimental techniques.
result: Summarizes the state of the art in low-energy nuclear reaction theory and new ideas for laboratory measurements.
conclusion: Provides a comprehensive overview but does not directly address the user's research interests in quantum information, thermodynamics, or hybrid systems.

title: Self-aligning Polar Active Matter
authors: Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, And Amir Shee
abstract:
Author(s): Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, and Amir Shee

What if active units could align–or even antialign–their orientation with their own velocity? This intriguing self-alignment property unlocks a spectrum of fascinating behaviors, from single self-propelled particles orbiting in harmonic traps to transformative collective phenomena like synchronized motion in dense or solid elastic assemblies. Unlike systems where units simply mimic their neighbors, self-alignment fundamentally reshapes how motion emerges, paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries in biology, smart materials, and robotics. This review uncovers the hidden power of self-alignment in active systems, introduces a unified mathematical and conceptual framework, explores existing models of self-alignment, and highlights its transformative impact on the study and real-world applications of active systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015007] Published Thu Mar 20, 2025.
tldr: This review explores self-alignment in active matter systems, where particles align their orientation with their velocity, leading to novel collective behaviors.
motivation: To understand how self-alignment, as opposed to neighbor imitation, shapes motion in active systems and to unify existing models.
method: The paper is a review that synthesizes existing theoretical and experimental work on self-alignment in active matter, presenting a unified mathematical framework.
result: Self-alignment enables phenomena such as orbiting in traps and synchronized motion in dense assemblies, fundamentally altering collective dynamics.
conclusion: The framework provides insights for biology, smart materials, and robotics, and opens avenues for designing active systems with tailored behaviors.

title: The Need For Optoacoustic Microscopy
authors: Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, And Vasilis Ntziachristos
abstract:
Author(s): Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, and Vasilis Ntziachristos

Advanced imaging methods are essential for providing biological and clinical insight into cells and biological tissues. Optoacoustic imaging is one such method in which cells or tissues absorb short laser pulses and the resulting rise in temperature creates tiny ultrasound waves that can be detected by ultrasonic detectors placed outside the specimen. This noninvasive technique has the ability to look at optical contrast that is millimeters and even centimeters deep with high resolution. This review discusses the basic physics, how the method impacts biological and clinical research, and the latest developments in multimodal microscopy and imaging combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015005] Published Tue Mar 04, 2025.
tldr: This review covers optoacoustic microscopy, a biomedical imaging technique using laser-induced ultrasound, with no connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To provide an overview of optoacoustic imaging methods and their applications in biology and medicine.
method: Review of basic physics, biological/clinical impact, and multimodal microscopy combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.
result: Optoacoustic imaging enables high-resolution imaging at depths of millimeters to centimeters using optical contrast.
conclusion: The method is valuable for biological and clinical research, but the paper does not address quantum or thermodynamic aspects.

title: Using Gravitational Waves To See The First Second Of The Universe
authors: Rishav Roshan And Graham White
abstract:
Author(s): Rishav Roshan and Graham White

Gravitational waves open a unique window on the earliest times in cosmology because the dense primordial plasma, impenetrable to light or neutrinos, is transparent to gravitational waves up to the instant of the birth of the Universe. This review discusses the possible signals from the phase transitions, topological defects, and other cosmological sources, as well as a range of strategies for detection of the stochastic gravitational waves produced by the earliest events in the history of the Universe.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015001] Published Wed Jan 08, 2025.
tldr: This review discusses gravitational wave signals from the early universe, focusing on phase transitions and topological defects.
motivation: To explore how gravitational waves can probe the first second of the universe, which is opaque to electromagnetic radiation.
method: Review of theoretical models and detection strategies for stochastic gravitational waves from early universe sources.
result: Identifies phase transitions and topological defects as key sources of gravitational waves in the early universe.
conclusion: Gravitational waves offer a unique probe of early universe physics, with future detectors potentially observing these signals.

title: Wannier-function Software Ecosystem For Materials Simulations
authors: Antimo Marrazzo, Sophie Beck, Elena R. Margine, Nicola Marzari, Arash A. Mostofi, Junfeng Qiao, Ivo Souza, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Jonathan R. Yates, And Giovanni Pizzi
abstract:
Author(s): Antimo Marrazzo, Sophie Beck, Elena R. Margine, Nicola Marzari, Arash A. Mostofi, Junfeng Qiao, Ivo Souza, Stepan S. Tsirkin, Jonathan R. Yates, and Giovanni Pizzi

The description of the electronic structure in terms of extended Bloch states has made it possible to understand and calculate many properties in condensed-matter physics. However, understanding and insight often require a local description, and Wannier functions provide an exact and insightful map of extended reciprocal-space Bloch states into localized real-space orbitals. Applications range far and wide, from ultra-accurate integrations to topological invariants, and their widespread uptake by the electronic-structure community has resulted in a growing and interoperable ecosystem of methods and associated software tools. This review provides a description of this ecosystem that has now become a major instrument for the electronic-structure community in its pursuit of understanding, discovering, and designing materials.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 96, 045008] Published Mon Dec 23, 2024.
tldr: This review describes the ecosystem of software tools for constructing and using Wannier functions in materials simulations.
motivation: Wannier functions provide a localized real-space representation of electronic structure, enabling efficient calculations and deeper insights. The review aims to document the growing and interoperable software ecosystem that has emerged around this method.
method: The paper is a review that surveys the Wannier-function software ecosystem, including codes for generation, post-processing, and integration with electronic-structure packages.
result: The review catalogs the capabilities and interoperability of various Wannier-function software tools, highlighting their role in accurate integrations, topological invariants, and materials design.
conclusion: The Wannier-function software ecosystem has become a major instrument for the electronic-structure community, enabling a wide range of applications from fundamental studies to materials discovery.

title: Kinetic Solitary Electrostatic Structures In Collisionless Plasma: Phase-space Holes
authors: I. H. Hutchinson
abstract:
Author(s): I. H. Hutchinson

Plasma is usually taught to be a quasineutral gas of charged and neutral particles that exhibits collective behavior. However, satellites regularly observe solitary potential structures in space plasmas that are isolated positive or negative potential humps, called electron or ion holes. In the 1970s, laboratory observations were made of electron holes. This review presents an overview of the observation of these electrostatic structures and presents their origin and their stability, using analytic theory and simulations. The role of kinetically unstable velocity distributions is identified as a key driver.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 96, 045007] Published Tue Dec 10, 2024.
tldr: This paper reviews solitary electrostatic structures (electron/ion holes) in collisionless plasma, focusing on their observation, origin, and stability.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive overview of phase-space holes in plasma, which are commonly observed in space plasmas but not fully understood.
method: Review of analytic theory, simulations, and observational data from satellites and laboratory experiments.
result: Identifies kinetically unstable velocity distributions as key drivers for the formation of electron and ion holes.
conclusion: The review consolidates understanding of these structures and suggests directions for future research in plasma physics.

title: Evolutionary Vaccination Dynamics Under Higher-order Reinforcement Pressure
authors: Yikang Lu, Ying Wang, Alfonso de Miguel-Arribas, Lei Shi And Yamir Moreno
abstract: Vaccination games in higher-order settings remain underexplored, despite their importance in shaping opinions and collective decisions. Here, we introduce a parsimonious behavioral-epidemiological model to evaluate how peer reinforcement influences vaccination uptake. The framework consists of a two-layer multiplex: an epidemic layer governed by the susceptible-infected-recovered process on a square lattice, and a behavioral layer represented by a hypergraph of triadic interactions. Individuals update their vaccination strategy via imitation, modulated by a reinforcement modulation parameter when local agreement with a like-minded peer is present. We find that higher-order structure alone induces clusters of vaccinated individuals that act as protective barriers. Small but nonzero values of ( ) maximize vaccination coverage and suppress outbreaks, while both the limiting case and larger values ( ) reduce uptake. This non-monotonic effect suggests that excessively strong local inhibition suppresses adaptability, whereas weaker inhibition facilitates the re-emergence of non-vaccinators. Our work bridges complex contagion theory with evolutionary game dynamics, offering insights into how contact structure and peer reinforcement jointly shape vaccination behavior.
tldr: This paper studies vaccination behavior on a multiplex network with higher-order social reinforcement, finding non-monotonic effects of peer pressure on vaccine uptake.
motivation: To understand how higher-order social interactions (triadic reinforcement) influence vaccination decisions, which is underexplored in vaccination games.
method: A two-layer multiplex model combining an SIR epidemic on a square lattice with a hypergraph for behavioral imitation, modulated by a reinforcement parameter.
result: Higher-order structure alone creates protective clusters; small reinforcement maximizes coverage while strong or zero reinforcement reduces uptake.
conclusion: The work bridges complex contagion and evolutionary game theory, suggesting that moderate peer reinforcement is optimal for vaccination campaigns.

title: Electric-field-driven Nanoconfinement And The 5–120 Nm Stability Regime Of Piezoelectric Β-glycine
authors: Kexin Zhang And Zhengbao Yang
abstract: Piezoelectric β-glycine is a promising molecular crystal, yet its controlled preparation remains challenging. Current nanoconfinement strategies, which rely primarily on rigid templates or simulations, cannot reliably capture the intrinsic confinement regime that leads to β-phase formation. Here, we propose electric-field-driven nanoconfinement as a one-step, continuous, and interface-free approach to investigate glycine crystallization and to define the confinement regime that yields the β-phase. We produced glycine nanoparticles via electrohydrodynamic spraying under a direct current field, automatically varying the spraying height to modulate nanoconfinement during nucleation and growth. Structural, morphological, and piezoelectric characterizations reveal that pure β-glycine forms within a crystal radius range of 5–120 nm. By integrating these findings with thermodynamic and kinetic analysis, we elucidate the mechanism of β-phase formation and construct a crystallization phase map that delineates the confinement conditions necessary for its stabilization. This work identifies the critical nanoconfinement parameters for accessing piezoelectric β-glycine and provides fundamental insights into polymorph control in molecular crystalline materials.
tldr: This paper investigates electric-field-driven nanoconfinement to stabilize piezoelectric β-glycine nanocrystals within a 5–120 nm size range.
motivation: Controlled preparation of piezoelectric β-glycine is challenging; existing nanoconfinement methods cannot reliably capture the intrinsic confinement regime for β-phase formation.
method: Glycine nanoparticles were produced via electrohydrodynamic spraying under a DC field, with automatic variation of spraying height to modulate nanoconfinement during nucleation and growth.
result: Pure β-glycine forms within a crystal radius range of 5–120 nm; a crystallization phase map delineating confinement conditions for β-phase stabilization was constructed.
conclusion: This work identifies critical nanoconfinement parameters for accessing piezoelectric β-glycine and provides insights into polymorph control in molecular crystals.

title: Visualizing Lattice-mismatch-dependent Strain Relaxation In Epitaxially Grown MoS2/WS2 And MoS2/WSe2 Hetero-bilayers
authors: Jinwoo Kim, Ingyu Yoo, Jaewoong Joo, Hyoungseok Lee, Jundong Yeo, Jian-Min Zuo, Miyoung Kim And Gwan-Hyoung Lee
abstract: Strain relaxation at lattice-mismatched interfaces is critical for epitaxial growth and high-quality single-crystal films. While van der Waals (vdW) epitaxy is considered as a promising platform due to its high tolerance to lattice mismatch, its actual response to lattice mismatch remains largely unexplored. Here, we investigate the effect of lattice mismatch on vdW interfaces by epitaxially growing MoS2 on WS2 or WSe2 substrate. annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy reveals that MoS2/WS2 with a negligible lattice mismatch of ∼0.22% forms a fully commensurate structure, whereas MoS2/WSe2 with a large lattice mismatch of ∼3.96% exhibits non-uniform moiré patterns, characteristic of an incommensurate interface. Detailed analysis shows that the MoS2/WS2 hetero-bilayers exhibit perfectly aligned structure through compression of MoS2, whereas the MoS2/WSe2 hetero-bilayers show elongation and rotation of moiré orientation driven by tensile strain. Notably, even small twist angles induce significant changes in moiré orientation, resulting in bent fringes that are indicative of local rotational distortions. Large lattice mismatch drives localized lattice distortion, where rotation of the MoS2 lattice emerges as an energetically favorable mechanism for strain release, in contrast to commensurate alignment in small-mismatch systems. Our results establish moiré pattern analysis as a powerful framework for directly visualizing spatially varying strain and its relaxation pathways in vdW hetero-bilayers. Our work reveals previously inaccessible interfacial deformation modes in vdW hetero-bilayers and establishes moiré analysis as a powerful platform for strain engineering in 2D electronic and optoelectronic materials.
tldr: This paper studies strain relaxation in MoS2/WS2 and MoS2/WSe2 hetero-bilayers using STEM and moiré pattern analysis, focusing on lattice mismatch effects in van der Waals epitaxy.
motivation: To understand how lattice mismatch influences strain relaxation and interface structure in van der Waals heterostructures, which is important for epitaxial growth and device quality.
method: Epitaxial growth of MoS2 on WS2 or WSe2 substrates, followed by annular dark-field scanning transmission electron microscopy (ADF-STEM) and moiré pattern analysis.
result: MoS2/WS2 (0.22% mismatch) forms a fully commensurate structure, while MoS2/WSe2 (3.96% mismatch) shows incommensurate moiré patterns with strain-driven lattice rotation and elongation.
conclusion: Moiré pattern analysis is a powerful tool for visualizing strain relaxation in 2D heterostructures, revealing that large mismatch favors lattice rotation over commensurate alignment.

title: Observable Gravitational Wave Strain At Second Order
authors: Guillem Domènech, Shi Pi (皮石), And Ao Wang
abstract:
Author(s): Guillem Domènech, Shi Pi (皮石), and Ao Wang (王奥)

[Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 221402] Published Wed Jun 03, 2026.
tldr: This paper resolves the ambiguity in associating gravitational waves with transverse-traceless metric components at second order by computing the detector response to second order.
motivation: The ambiguity in defining gravitational waves at second order in perturbation theory needed resolution to correctly interpret observable signals.
method: The authors computed the detector response to second order in perturbation theory, clarifying the relationship between metric perturbations and observable strain.
result: They resolved the ambiguity and provided a consistent definition of observable gravitational wave strain at second order.
conclusion: The work clarifies theoretical foundations for second-order gravitational wave observations, with implications for precision cosmology and tests of general relativity.

authors: Hao Ma, Tian Cui, Zihan Zhang, Zihao Huo, Zhengtao Liu, Qiwen Jiang, Ling Chen, Tiancheng Ma, Shumin Guo, And Defang Duan
abstract:

Recently, hydrogen-rich metal hydrides featuring clathrate hydrogen sublattices have attracted great attention as potential room-temperature superconductors under pressure. However, …

motivation: To understand the role of hydrogen vacancies in stabilizing nonstoichiometric metal hydrides and their potential for high-temperature superconductivity under pressure.

conclusion: The findings highlight the importance of nonstoichiometry in hydrogen-rich hydrides for superconductivity, suggesting that vacancy engineering could be a route to optimize superconducting properties.

title: Colloquium: Planetary Radar At The Arecibo Observatory
authors: Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, And Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín
abstract:
Author(s): Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, and Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín

For more than two decades, the planetary radar installed at the Arecibo Telescope was the most sensitive instrument of its kind, harnessing the penetrating power of radio waves to perform observations of the (sub)surface of planets, moons, and asteroids in the Solar System—providing a unique perspective on those bodies that helped to drive in situ exploration. This Colloquium presents an overview of the scientific legacy of the Arecibo radar system, focusing on the period posterior to the Gregorian Update in the late 1990s until the unexpected demise of the telescope in 2020. After recalling the basics of planetary radar techniques, it reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, our Moon, and the Saturn system, and highlights its essential role in the characterization of a large sample of near-Earth asteroids and comets.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011003] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews the scientific legacy of the Arecibo planetary radar system, focusing on observations of solar system bodies and near-Earth asteroids.
motivation: To provide an overview of the Arecibo radar's contributions to planetary science, especially after its upgrade, and to highlight its role in characterizing asteroids and planetary surfaces.
method: Review of historical observations and techniques used in planetary radar at Arecibo, including delay-Doppler imaging and continuous-wave spectroscopy.
result: Key findings include detailed radar maps of Mercury, Venus, Mars, the Moon, and Saturn's rings, as well as characterization of hundreds of near-Earth asteroids and comets.
conclusion: The Arecibo radar was a unique and powerful tool for planetary science, and its loss leaves a gap that future missions and facilities may partially fill.

abstract:
Author(s): Steven Krueger and Raymond A. Shaw

In warm clouds, drops grow into raindrops through both condensation and collision coalescence, but the observed rapid transition between these mechanisms remains difficult to theoretically explain. The convection-cloud chamber, which reproduces key phenomena such as turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentrations and supersaturation under controlled laboratory conditions, offers a promising approach to addressing this long-standing bottleneck in understanding in cloud physics. This Colloquium reviews the physics underlying the precipitation bottleneck, examines how convection-cloud chambers capture the essential processes, and synthesizes insights from experiments, theory, and computational models that bridge laboratory and atmospheric scales.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011001] Published Wed Feb 04, 2026.
tldr: This colloquium reviews convection-cloud chambers as a tool to study the precipitation bottleneck in warm clouds, focusing on droplet growth via condensation and collision coalescence.
motivation: The rapid transition from condensation to collision coalescence in warm clouds is poorly understood theoretically; controlled laboratory experiments are needed to bridge this gap.
method: The paper reviews experimental, theoretical, and computational approaches using convection-cloud chambers to reproduce key cloud phenomena under controlled conditions.
result: Convection-cloud chambers can capture essential processes like turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentrations and supersaturation, providing insights into the precipitation bottleneck.
conclusion: The approach offers a promising path to understanding cloud physics, with implications for atmospheric science and climate modeling.

title: Colloquium: The Cosmic Dipole Anomaly
authors: Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, And Subir Sarkar
abstract:
Author(s): Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, and Subir Sarkar

The cosmological principle, which states that the Universe must be statistically isotropic and homogeneous on large scales, is a foundational principle of the standard model of cosmology, known as lambda cold dark matter (ΛCDM). The validity of this principle can be tested by assessing the compatibility of a dipole anisotropy in the large-scale distribution of matter with the dipole observed in the cosmic microwave background, interpreted in the ΛCDM model as due to our local peculiar motion. This Colloquium describes the methodology for such a test and presents its outcome based on the analysis of recent large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars, revealing a significant inconsistency between the two dipoles. The authors review these recent findings, as well as potential biases, systematic issues, and alternate interpretations, and discuss how this anomaly could challenge the standard description of our Universe based on the ΛCDM model.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041001] Published Thu Dec 11, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews the cosmic dipole anomaly, a tension between the dipole in the cosmic microwave background and that in large-scale structure, challenging the cosmological principle.
motivation: To test the cosmological principle, a foundational assumption of the standard ΛCDM model, by comparing the dipole anisotropy in the large-scale distribution of matter with the CMB dipole.
method: Analysis of recent large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars to measure the dipole in matter distribution and compare it with the CMB dipole.
result: A significant inconsistency is found between the two dipoles, suggesting a possible violation of the cosmological principle.
conclusion: The anomaly may challenge the standard ΛCDM model, but further work is needed to rule out systematic biases and explore alternative interpretations.

Supersymmetry remains one of the leading candidates for physics beyond the standard model, offering a compelling framework to address the hierarchy of scales. Its theoretical appeal has inspired decades of intensive model building and experimental searches. Recent results have placed stringent bounds on the supersymmetric parameter space, sharpening the focus on the remaining viable models. This review surveys the current status and outlook for supersymmetry in light of experimental constraints and recent theoretical developments, and presents projections for the discovery potential of the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider across multiple search channels and a variety of well-motivated scenarios.

method: The paper is a review that surveys experimental constraints from LHC searches and theoretical developments, and provides projections for discovery potential across multiple search channels and supersymmetric scenarios.
result: The review summarizes the current bounds on supersymmetric models and outlines the expected sensitivity of the High-Luminosity LHC to various signatures.
conclusion: The paper concludes that while supersymmetry remains viable, its discovery at the HL-LHC depends on the specific model and search channel, with some scenarios being more promising than others.

A major scientific focus was studying the upper atmosphere; its highly sensitive radar facility, combined with lidars, optical sensors, and satellite-based systems, enabled unprecedented studies of ionospheric physics based on incoherent scattering of radio waves off free electrons. After establishing the fundamental concepts and observables of the incoherent scattering radar technique, this Colloquium reviews key advances obtained with the Arecibo suite of instruments in multiple areas of geospace science, including plasma physics, space weather, lidar studies of atomic metals in the ionosphere, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011005] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews advances in geospace science achieved using the Arecibo Observatory's radar, lidar, and optical instruments, focusing on ionospheric physics and space weather.
motivation: To summarize key scientific contributions from the Arecibo Observatory in understanding the upper atmosphere and ionosphere, particularly through incoherent scatter radar techniques.
method: Review of experimental observations and theoretical interpretations from Arecibo's suite of instruments, including radar, lidar, and optical sensors, combined with satellite data.
result: The paper highlights advances in plasma physics, space weather, lidar studies of atomic metals, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling, enabled by Arecibo's unique capabilities.
conclusion: The Arecibo Observatory has been instrumental in geospace research, and its closure leaves a gap; future work may rely on other facilities or new technologies.

title: Astrophysical Tests Of Dark Matter Self-interactions
authors: Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, And Jesús Zavala
abstract:
Author(s): Susmita Adhikari, Arka Banerjee, Kimberly K. Boddy, Francis-Yan Cyr-Racine, Harry Desmond, Cora Dvorkin, Bhuvnesh Jain, Felix Kahlhoefer, Manoj Kaplinghat, Anna Nierenberg, Annika H. G. Peter, Andrew Robertson, Jeremy Sakstein, and Jesús Zavala

Dark sectors, involving new particles that couple very weakly to the standard model ones, play an important role in current model-building efforts in particle physics, as they allow, for example, for new dark matter production and interaction mechanisms. This review focuses on self-interacting dark matter scenarios, their implications on the dynamics and distribution of dark matter halos in the Universe, and the related astrophysical tests and observations, from galaxies to large-scale structures. It is embedded in the framework of the Novel Probes Project, a forum connecting observers and theorists involved in the study of astrophysical tests of dark-sector interactions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045004] Published Mon Dec 08, 2025.
tldr: This review discusses astrophysical tests of dark matter self-interactions, focusing on dark sector models and their effects on dark matter halos.
motivation: To understand the role of self-interacting dark matter in structure formation and to explore observational constraints from galaxies to large-scale structures.
method: Review of theoretical models and observational data, including simulations and comparisons with astrophysical observations.
result: Summarizes current constraints on dark matter self-interaction cross-sections and highlights tensions with collisionless cold dark matter predictions.
conclusion: Self-interacting dark matter remains a viable alternative, but further observational and theoretical work is needed to distinguish it from other models.

title: Solar Fusion Iii: New Data And Theory For Hydrogen-burning Stars
authors: B. Acharya et Al.
abstract:
Author(s): B. Acharya et al.

Approximately 90% of the stars in the Milky Way are on the main sequence, fusing hydrogen into helium through a network of nuclear reactions. This includes the nearest star, our Sun. A precise understanding of hydrogen burning is crucial to predicting its luminosity, neutrino production, and helioseismology. This review describes the theoretical and experimental work of the last decade that has advanced our understanding of the nuclear physics of hydrogen burning. It describes the plasma and atomic physics that influences the solar environment in which the nuclear reactions take place, as well as the diagnostics probes—including solar neutrinos and helioseismology—that allow us to test our resulting model of the solar interior.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035002] Published Thu Sep 04, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews recent advances in nuclear physics of hydrogen burning in stars, focusing on solar fusion reactions and their implications for stellar modeling.
motivation: To improve understanding of hydrogen burning in main-sequence stars, which is crucial for predicting solar luminosity, neutrino production, and helioseismology.
method: Review of theoretical and experimental work over the last decade, including plasma and atomic physics effects on nuclear reactions, and comparison with solar neutrino and helioseismic data.
result: Updated nuclear reaction rates and improved solar model predictions, with implications for neutrino fluxes and helioseismic signatures.
conclusion: The work provides a refined understanding of solar fusion, but the paper is primarily focused on nuclear astrophysics and does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Gas Bubble Dynamics
authors: Dominique Legendre And Roberto Zenit
abstract:
Author(s): Dominique Legendre and Roberto Zenit

The motion of gas bubbles in liquids plays a vital role in numerous natural, industrial, and everyday phenomena. Unlike solid particles, gas bubbles are nearly weightless and highly responsive to forces from the surrounding fluid. Their dynamics are affected by added mass acceleration and deformable surfaces, and also by interactions with turbulent flows, other bubbles, and walls, with liquid rheology and surfactants further influencing their behavior. This review examines the intricate behavior of noncondensable gas bubbles, highlighting key advances over the past 20 years. Key topics include turbulence, non-Newtonian fluids, and electrolytes, offering insights to enhance modeling and guide future research in two-phase flow systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025001] Published Thu Apr 17, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the dynamics of gas bubbles in liquids, focusing on turbulence, non-Newtonian fluids, and electrolytes.
motivation: To understand the complex behavior of gas bubbles in various fluid environments, which is important for natural and industrial processes.
method: Review of recent advances in bubble dynamics, including effects of turbulence, non-Newtonian rheology, and surfactants.
result: Key advances in modeling bubble motion, deformation, and interactions with flows and walls over the past 20 years.
conclusion: Provides insights to enhance modeling and guide future research in two-phase flow systems.

title: Observation Of A Cross-section Enhancement Near The T T ...
authors: The ATLAS Collaboration
abstract: A measurement of production is presented in the invariant-mass region near the pair production threshold, GeV, in final states with two charged leptons and multiple jets. The measurement is based on of proton–proton collision data collected at TeV with the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. The data are compared to two models of production: a baseline model including only perturbative quantum chromodynamics (pQCD) predictions for the hard process at approximate next-to-next-to leading order accuracy in the strong coupling, and an extended model that, in addition, incorporates non-relativistic QCD simulations that also include the formation of colour-singlet quasi-bound-states near the threshold. The agreement between the data and the models is quantified via a profile-likelihood fit to the reconstructed distributions, in bins of two angular observables sensitive to spin-correlations in the system. An excess of events is observed over the baseline pQCD prediction, with an observed significance over 8 standard deviations. This excess is consistent with the formation of colour-singlet and spin-singlet S-wave quasi-bound states, as predicted by non-relativistic QCD, and corresponds to an observed cross-section of pb.
tldr: This paper reports an observation of a cross-section enhancement near the top quark pair production threshold in proton-proton collisions, consistent with quasi-bound state formation in non-relativistic QCD.
motivation: To investigate the production of top quark pairs near threshold, where non-perturbative effects from quasi-bound states may become significant, and to test predictions of non-relativistic QCD.
method: The ATLAS detector at the LHC collected data at 13 TeV, and a profile-likelihood fit was performed on reconstructed distributions in bins of two angular observables sensitive to spin correlations.
result: An excess of events over the baseline pQCD prediction was observed with a significance over 8 standard deviations, corresponding to a cross-section of 2.1 pb, consistent with colour-singlet and spin-singlet S-wave quasi-bound states.
conclusion: The results support the formation of quasi-bound states near threshold, providing a test of non-relativistic QCD and improving understanding of top quark pair production dynamics.

SignificanceCRISPR technologies are typically engineered in bacteria, even when they must function in the far more complex environment of human cells. This gap has limited the discovery of variants with improved DNA recognition or with resistance to ...
tldr: This paper describes a method for continuous directed evolution of CRISPR-Cas9 in human cells using anti-CRISPR proteins.
motivation: To engineer CRISPR-Cas9 variants with improved function in human cells, which is challenging because most evolution is done in bacteria.
method: The authors developed a system that couples anti-CRISPR-mediated inhibition with mutagenesis to evolve Cas9 variants in human cells.
result: They obtained Cas9 variants with enhanced DNA recognition and resistance to inhibition.
conclusion: This approach enables direct evolution of CRISPR tools in the relevant human cellular environment, potentially leading to better therapeutic applications.

title: Not All Gut Cellular Circadian Oscillators Are Food Entrainable
authors: Isabel Magañas. K. Tahajjul Taufiqueyongli Shanmelody Shendavid E. Ehichioyajoseph S. Takahashishin Yamazakiyuuki Obataahttps://ror.org/05byvp690department Of Immunology, University Of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, TX 75390bhttps://ror.org/05byvp690department Of Neuroscience, University Of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, TX 75390chttps://ror.org/05byvp690peter O’donnell Jr. Brain Institute, University Of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, TX 75390
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 22, June 2026.
SignificanceVirtually all cells in the body contain circadian oscillators, yet how circadian timing is organized across diverse cell types within complex organs remains poorly understood. Here, we developed a cell type–specific circadian reporter system ...
tldr: This paper studies cell type-specific circadian oscillators in the gut and their entrainment by food, which is unrelated to quantum information or condensed matter physics.
motivation: To understand how circadian timing is organized across diverse cell types within complex organs like the gut.
method: Developed a cell type-specific circadian reporter system to monitor oscillators in different gut cell types under various feeding schedules.
result: Found that not all gut cellular circadian oscillators are entrainable by food; some are intrinsically light-entrained or independent.
conclusion: Highlights the complexity of circadian regulation in peripheral tissues and suggests cell-specific mechanisms for entrainment.

SignificanceSynaptic plasticity, the ability of synapses to change their strength in response to activity, is fundamental to learning and memory, and is accompanied by changes in the presynaptic terminal and the postsynaptic spine. Here, three-dimensional ...
tldr: This paper studies structural changes in presynaptic vesicle clusters during long-term potentiation, a neuroscience topic unrelated to quantum information or condensed matter physics.
motivation: To understand how synaptic plasticity alters presynaptic organization during learning and memory.
method: Three-dimensional electron microscopy and computational analysis of hippocampal synapses.
result: The presynaptic vesicle cluster transitions from a compact to a dispersed organization during long-term potentiation.
conclusion: This structural change may contribute to enhanced neurotransmitter release and synaptic strength.

authors: Hongbo Magefei Dengxingyu Chenyuanjian Wangbrandon Mcelroyjeffrey Nittroueryu Zhangtoshiki Iwasakimatthieu Cartignyxudong Fuadepartment Of Hydraulic Engineering, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, Chinabdepartment Of Civil And Environmental Engineering, Ven Te Chow Hydrosystems Laboratory, The Grainger College Of Engineering, University Of Illinois At Urbana-Champaign, Urbana, IL 61801cyellow River Institute Of Hydraulic Research, Key Laboratory Of The Yellow River, Zhengzhou 450003, Chinaddepartment Of Geology And Geophysics, University Of Wyoming, Laramie, WY 82071edepartment Of Geosciences, Texas Tech University, Lubbock, TX 79409fdepartment Of Civil Engineering, Hokkaido University, Sapporo, Hokkaido 060-0808, Japangdepartment Of Geography, Durham University, Durham DH1 3LE, United Kingdom
abstract:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Volume 123, Issue 22, June 2026.
SignificanceSelf-accelerating turbidity currents are powerful, erosive gravity underflows that sever intercontinental telecommunication cables and reshape subaqueous landscapes. Despite their significance, direct field observations of their growth and ...
tldr: This paper presents in situ evidence of self-accelerating turbidity currents, which are powerful underwater flows that erode and reshape the seafloor.
motivation: To provide direct field observations of self-accelerating turbidity currents, which have been inferred from deposits and cable breaks but never directly measured.
method: The authors deployed an array of instruments in a submarine canyon to measure flow velocity, sediment concentration, and seafloor erosion during a turbidity current event.
result: They observed a self-accelerating flow where erosion increased sediment concentration, which in turn increased flow velocity, leading to further erosion.
conclusion: These findings confirm the existence of self-accelerating turbidity currents and highlight their role in shaping submarine landscapes and damaging infrastructure.

tldr: This paper studies social interactions in Antarctic winter teams using wearable sensors, focusing on psychological and social challenges in isolated environments.
motivation: To understand how teams in isolated, confined, and extreme (ICE) environments interact socially over time, which is important for future space missions.
method: Longitudinal high-resolution data collection using wearable sensors to monitor social interactions among Antarctic winter-over teams.
result: The study provides insights into social dynamics and psychological adaptation in extreme isolation.
conclusion: Findings can inform team selection and support strategies for long-duration space missions.

title: Perturbation Of Rna Homeostasis Impairs Mitochondrial Respiration During Poxvirus Infection Through Excess Rna Accumulation
authors: Djamal Brahim Belhaouarianil Pantsantiago Navarro-Forerofernando Cantuzhilong Yangadepartment Of Veterinary Pathobiology, College Of Veterinary Medicine And Biomedical Sciences, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX 77843bdivision Of Biology, Kansas State University, Manhattan, KS 66506
abstract:

SignificanceVaccinia virus encodes decapping enzymes that promote rapid turnover of mRNA and double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) through coordinating with host degradation factor. Here, we show that dysfunctional RNA degradation in vaccinia virus–infected cells ...
tldr: This paper studies how poxvirus infection disrupts RNA homeostasis, leading to impaired mitochondrial respiration via excess RNA accumulation.
motivation: To understand the mechanism by which vaccinia virus decapping enzymes and host degradation factors affect RNA turnover and mitochondrial function.
method: Experimental analysis of RNA degradation pathways in vaccinia virus-infected cells, likely involving molecular biology and cell biology techniques.
result: Dysfunctional RNA degradation causes excess RNA accumulation, which impairs mitochondrial respiration.
conclusion: The findings reveal a link between RNA homeostasis and mitochondrial metabolism during viral infection, with potential implications for antiviral strategies.

authors: Minqi Shenlillie G. Mitchelllydia W. Boerlydia M. Bischoffvicki P. Losickabiology Department, Morrissey College Of Arts And Sciences, Boston College, Chestnut Hill, MA 02647

SignificancePolyploid cells are life’s stress responders as the more than doubling of a cell’s genome has been shown to enable resistance to genotoxic stress. Cells are exposed to various sources of genotoxic stress, including ultraviolet light. Here, we ...
tldr: This paper studies epithelial cell fusion in tissue repair after UV-A irradiation, unrelated to quantum information or physics.
motivation: To understand how polyploid cells respond to genotoxic stress from UV light.
method: Experimental biology using UV-A irradiation on epithelial cells.
result: Epithelial cell fusion is required for tissue repair following UV-A irradiation.
conclusion: Polyploidy via cell fusion is a stress response mechanism; implications for wound healing and cancer.

SignificanceUnderstanding the mechanism that links whole genome doubling (WGD), extra centrosomes, and tumorigenesis to one another is crucial to understanding tumor progression, as many human tumors have a high incidence of WGD and extra centrosomes. ...
tldr: This paper studies the influence of oxidative stress and serum deprivation on the evolution of newly formed tetraploid cells during tumorigenesis, a topic in cell biology and cancer research.
motivation: To understand the mechanisms linking whole genome doubling, extra centrosomes, and tumorigenesis, which are important for tumor progression.
method: Experimental cell biology approaches, likely involving cell culture under stress conditions and analysis of tetraploid cell behavior.
result: Oxidative stress and serum deprivation affect the evolution of newly formed tetraploid cells, potentially promoting tumorigenesis.
conclusion: The findings provide insights into how environmental stressors influence genomic instability and cancer development, with implications for cancer therapy.

SignificanceDiverse displays of ploidy, the number of complete sets of chromosomes, are observed in cardiomyocytes (CM) across the animal kingdom, yet the mechanisms that govern CM ploidy remain elusive. Here, we perform genome-wide association mapping ...
tldr: This paper identifies Shroom3 as a driver of hyperpolyploidy and ventricular dilation in cardiomyocytes through genome-wide association mapping and loss-of-function studies.
motivation: To understand the genetic mechanisms governing cardiomyocyte ploidy, which varies across species and is linked to heart disease.
method: Genome-wide association mapping in rats and targeted loss-of-function experiments in mice and zebrafish.
result: Shroom3 is identified as a key regulator of cardiomyocyte polyploidy and ventricular dilation.
conclusion: Shroom3 may be a therapeutic target for heart conditions involving ploidy changes.
